verses.note: The verses show sin's instinct to explain rather than confess. The rest of Scripture treats honest confession as the way back to God (Psalm 32:5, 1 John 1:9), exactly what neither the man nor the woman offers here.
God warns before he judges. The questions are an invitation to turn back while the choice is still open, the same pattern the prophets follow when they call Israel to do well before judgment falls.

Hebrews 12:17 says that Esau afterward sought the blessing with tears but ‘found no place for repentance’. Interpreters disagree whether the repentance he could not find was a change of mind in Isaac (so the blessing could be reversed) or genuine repentance in Esau himself. Either reading warns that some choices, once made, have consequences that tears alone do not undo.

Jacob does not say he is sorry, and the text does not put a confession in his mouth. What he does is return, under the name ‘gift’, something called by the very word he stole in chapter 27. The Old Testament's idea of turning back often takes this shape: a wrong not only regretted but repaired in kind.

Repentance here is concrete and communal. The household does not only feel differently about other gods; it hands them over, washes, and dresses differently. The same shape recurs at Sinai (Exodus 19:10) and in Israel's later renewals.

Judah's confession has the elements the Bible later looks for in repentance: he admits the fault publicly, names the specific wrong, and stops the behavior. The same man will later offer himself as a slave for Benjamin (44:33), which shows the confession was not a single moment of embarrassment.

The brothers do not blame Egypt, the famine, or their father. They name a specific wrong, a specific victim, and their own refusal to listen, which is how genuine repentance begins in Scripture, even before it is complete.

The steward's offer recreates the choice of Genesis 37: save yourselves and leave Rachel's son to slavery. Repentance is tested when the same door opens again, and the next verses show whether the brothers walk through it.
The brothers' return is the evidence the whole test was built to find. Twenty years earlier they left a brother to slavery and came home; now they refuse to go home without one.

Judah repeats his father's favoritism without complaint and repeats the story of Joseph's death without defending himself. The brothers' lie is exposed in Joseph's hearing by one of the men who told it.

For the first time the brothers name what they did to Joseph as pesha and chatta't, transgression and sin, and ask directly for forgiveness. Their confession in 42:21 was to one another; this one is made to the man they wronged.
Moses does not excuse the people; he names their stubbornness and includes himself (‘our iniquity’). The plea for forgiveness rests entirely on God's character, not on any promise of improvement.

The rite requires spoken confession. The goat does not carry away sins no one has named. Confession is built into the heart of Israel's most solemn ritual, which is why later Jewish teaching could insist that the day does not atone without repentance.

The people are not spectators of the priest's work. They fast and humble themselves while the rite is performed, so that God's provision is received by a people who acknowledge their need. Isaiah 58 later insists that such humbling must be joined to justice.

Suffering is presented as God's call to return, and the tragedy is that the call is not heard. The verse links repentance with seeking (darash) the LORD: turning away from sin is turning toward a person.

Ephraim asks God to turn him so that he can turn. Repentance in this verse is both God's gift and the person's act, and Christian traditions that stress grace (Augustine, the Reformers) and those that stress human response have both appealed to it. The shame of verse 19 is not the end of the confession; it is the sign that the discipline has done its work.

In this passage repentance follows the gift of a new heart; it does not earn it. The sequence is found also in Ezekiel 16:62-63, where God's atonement leads his people to remember and be silent from shame. Christian theology has debated whether repentance precedes or follows regeneration; this text places deep repentance after renewal.

Confession here is a covenant act. Leviticus 26:40-42 had made confession the condition on which God would remember his covenant with the patriarchs, so Daniel's confession is not self-reproach for its own sake but the prescribed road back to God.

The people's repentance takes the form of grief over the one they wounded, as intense as a parent's grief for an only child. Biblical repentance here is sorrow directed toward a person, not merely regret for consequences.

Repentance is corporate and personal at once: the whole land mourns, yet each family mourns apart. The leaders are named first, so those most responsible for the nation's direction lead the confession.

Receiving God's forgiveness and extending it belong together. The Reformed and Lutheran traditions stress that forgiving others is the fruit and evidence of forgiveness received; Catholic and Orthodox teaching speaks of it as part of the cooperation with grace that forgiveness requires. All treat the warning as real.
John's preaching makes repentance the doorway to the gospel. It is a turning of the whole person, publicly marked, and it looks toward forgiveness that God gives.
Confession of sin is spoken and public. The people do not only feel sorry; they say what they have done, which is the biblical shape of repentance from Leviticus 26:40 to 1 John 1:9.
Repentance and faith are joined as one response. To turn from sin and to trust the good news are two sides of the same turning toward God.
Jesus calls sinners, and the call assumes they need a physician. The verse joins mercy and diagnosis: no one is too sick to be called, and no one is healed who insists he is well.

Pastors have long pointed out, with Augustine and Bunyan, that those who fear they have committed this sin show by their very fear and longing for God that they have not; the sin described here does not grieve over itself. The warning is aimed at hardened opponents, not the anxious. Anyone tormented by this fear should not carry it alone but speak with a pastor or trusted believer, and, if the fear has become obsessive or crushing, with a counselor or doctor as well.

The apostles' first message is the call to repent, a turning of the whole life toward God. The verse places repentance at the center of Christian proclamation from its beginning, alongside acts of deliverance and healing that show what the turning is toward.

Herod hears John gladly and is troubled, but never acts on what he hears. The verses show that being moved by the word, even enjoying it, is not repentance; the parable of the soils (4:16-19) has already described such hearing.

Peter's tears are the beginning of repentance, not its end. Mark shows the leading apostle at his worst and does not soften it, and the risen Jesus names him in the message of 16:7. The church has seen in Peter's restoration (John 21:15-19) the proof that grave failure is not beyond grace.

Peter is not summoned because he has repented; the message goes to him before he has said a word. Mark's Gospel shows restoration beginning with the risen Lord's initiative toward the one who failed worst, which is why the way back for failed disciples is always an invitation before it is a demand.
Repentance here restores relationships: fathers to children, the disobedient to the wisdom of the righteous. Luke 3:10-14 will show what that turning looks like in practice.

John's baptism joins repentance and forgiveness. The verse defines the forgiveness God offers as received by turning, and the rest of John's preaching (verses 8-14) shows what the turning must include.
Repentance is proven by fruit. John will not accept a baptism that changes a person's status but not their conduct.
John does not tell the soldiers to leave their service but to stop abusing its power. Repentance is specific to one's position: each group hears the temptation of its own trade named.
The call to repent is itself good news, because it comes before the judgment, not after. John's warning is the last opportunity offered as a gift.

In the story the sheep does nothing but get found; in the application the found one is ‘one sinner who repents’. Luke's point is that repentance is the human side of being found by God. Amy-Jill Levine (Short Stories by Jesus, 2014) argues that neither sheep nor coin can repent and that Luke's applications in verses 7 and 10 narrow the stories; others answer that Luke never claims the sheep repents, only that the joy over finding it is the joy over a returning sinner.

Interpreters disagree about how pure the son's motive is. Many readers from the church fathers on see here the beginning of true repentance. Others, including Kenneth Bailey and Amy-Jill Levine, hear a hungry man calculating how to eat. The story may intend both: repentance often begins in need, and the father's welcome does not wait to test the motive.

The message to the nations is repentance and forgiveness in Jesus' name. The pairing of turning and pardon, preached first by John (3:3) and then by Jesus, becomes the content of the apostolic proclamation in Acts (2:38, 3:19, 26:20).

Jesus does not answer the request for water with a lecture, but he does not give the gift while leaving the woman's life untouched. The command to call her husband brings the truth of her circumstances into the light as part of receiving what he offers.
The word to go and sin no more shows that forgiveness is not indifference. The new life begins from being uncondemned, not from earning release, and it is still a life turned away from sin.

Repentance begins with the recognition of guilt that the truth produces, not with self-improvement. The crowd's question comes from conviction, and the answer Peter gives is not a program but a turn toward God.
Repentance is the first word of the church's first call. Metanoia in the New Testament is a change of mind that turns the whole person, rooted in the prophets' call to return (shuv) to the LORD.
Repentance is God's gift before it is our act: his kindness leads to it. God's delay in judgment is purposeful, and to treat it as permission is to reject the purpose (2 Peter 3:9).
Hardness of heart is not a fixed fate here but the refusal of an offer. Each day of unrepentance adds to what is stored, which makes the present an urgent time of mercy.

Repentance ‘from dead works’ stands first among the foundations, paired with faith toward God. The phrase returns in 9:14, where Christ's blood cleanses the conscience from dead works: the repentance the gospel begins with is made possible by the sacrifice it proclaims.

The verse speaks not of a single sin but of a settled turning away from the only sacrifice there is. Repentance is impossible here because the one who renounces Christ has renounced the ground of forgiveness itself; the author will say the same in 10:26-29.
